title: To my honoured friend Francis Godolphin of Godolphin
paragraphs: Your worthy brother Sidney Godolphin, while he lived, was pleased to think something of my studies. As you know, he also put me in his debt by giving me real proofs of his good opinion, great in themselves and greater still for the worth of the man who gave them. There was no virtue fitting a man to serve God or his country, to live in civil society or to be a friend in private, that did not plainly appear in his conduct. He did not acquire those virtues from necessity or put them on for an occasion; they belonged to his generous nature and shone through it. To honour and thank him, and as a mark of my devotion to you, I humbly dedicate to you this discourse on the commonwealth.

I do not know how the world will receive it, or what it may mean for those who seem to favour it. Where some contend on one side for too much liberty and others on the other for too much authority, it is hard to pass between their points unhurt. Yet I think the civil power ought not to condemn an attempt to advance it; nor should private people, by condemning the attempt, declare that they think that power too great. Besides, I speak not of particular men but of the seat of power in the abstract. I am like those simple and impartial creatures on the Roman Capitol who by their noise defended the people inside, not because of who they were, but because they were there. I think I offend only those outside, or any within who happen to favour them.

What may give most offence is that I cite certain passages of Holy Scripture for a purpose other than the one for which people usually cite them. But I have done it with due submission, and the subject made it necessary: these texts are the enemy’s outworks, from which they attack the civil power.

If, despite this, you find my work generally condemned, you can excuse yourself by saying that I love my own opinions and think everything I say is true; that I honoured your brother and honour you; and that on that basis I have presumed, without your knowledge, to call myself what I am:
Sir, your most humble and obedient servant, Thomas Hobbes.
